newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro woos foreign investors with concessions.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro woos foreign investors with concessions.

text.p: Montenegro's government is wooing foreign investment and is ready to offer state concessions as incentives, but analysts say its laws are still discouraging.
"Our government is prepared to offer state concessions for infrastructure construction in the republic," Montenegrin Foreign Minister Janko Jeknic told Reuters.
"There are projects on the construction of motorways, regional watersupply system, reconstruction of airports that allow for the possibility of state concessions," he said.
But distrustful local businessmen say the current openness to western capital by the government is just posturing ahead of the general election scheduled for early November.

"They just say they are for the open market economy," said one local businessman, who asked not to be named. "They may be for the open market economy but open only for their friends and acquaintances," he said.

Branislav Trgovic, assistant manager to state-owned hotel and tourist enterprise Milocer said the company has signed a concession contract worth 2.5 million German marks ($1.6 million) on the construction of tennis courts in this seaside resort.

"We have yielded part of our best beach Kraljicina Plaza (Queen's Beach) to a private company, Littlefield Enterprise Ltd, for 15 years to construct a tennis centre which could be used throughout the year," Trgovic said.
But it turned out the owner of the British company was a famous tennis player and a Yugoslav citizen -- Slobodan Zivojinovic.
Foreign investors also warned there will be no major foreign capital inflow into Montenegro unless it changed its proprerty laws to enable foreign companies to own land on which they could build.
"I know that German investors insist on the ownership of the land -- and that is not possible here," said a visiting German investment advisor who asked not to be named.
"It is absolutely necessary that the companies can be the owners of everything," he said.
Montenegrin officials said on Tuesday the legal framework for the fresh capital inflow from abroad exists.
"The current laws provide free market regulations and favourable conditions for foreign investments," Jeknic said.
German experts cautioned that Montenegro's advanced privatisation process, attractive investment projects and willingness to cooperate alone was not enough to attract foreign investors.

"German enterprises show big interest to engage in the revival of the economy here," they said "but also demand that foreign companies enjoy equal treatment and protection as local companies." ($1=1.5124 Mark)
